Accelerating industry competition, coupled with declining user activity, foreshadows an eventual price decline for Pandora (P).
As music streaming is becoming increasingly popular in comparison to radio-style listening, Pandora finds itself in big trouble. Sure, several years ago Pandora was the go-to platform for listening to music, but times have changed. Pandora faces massive competition from Apple Music (AAPL) and Spotify (SPOT), which have created subscription services that will effectively leave Pandora with nothing.
The reason for this is that Apple Music and Spotify are an inexpensive way to listen to music commercial-free. These two platforms are preferred over Pandora due to the inherent freedom associated with being able to listen to a specific song you want, when you want. Currently, you can’t do this on Pandora’s platform; instead, you only have the option of selecting a station/playlist similar to the song or genre you’re looking for. After deciding on a station and selecting it, you might realize that you don’t like the song that’s playing.
Unfortunately, there are a restricted number of options in terms of what you can do about it. Option number one: You can continue skipping songs (the number of skips are limited) until you find one you like, while having to pause and listen to commercials in between. Option number two: You can try a different station/playlist and hope you find what you’re looking for. A counterargument to this could be: What if someone prefers to leave their device on a playlist or radio station and continuously listen to music hands-off? Well, along with individual song selection, Apple Music and Spotify also offer the ability to listen to radio stations and smart playlists, essentially encompassing Pandora’s entire business model.
Same Price for a Worse Experience
Comparing the price difference between Pandora and its competitors, Apple music offers a student discount price of $4.99 per month, an individual price of $9.99 per month, and a family price of $14.99 per month. Spotify also offers services for students at a discount of $4.99 per month or a premium service of $9.99 per month. Pandora is trying it’s best impersonation by offering a premium feature where users pay a $9.99 monthly fee; however, unlike the other two platforms, Pandora still forces its users to watch a short video before listening.
Further justification of the social shift taking place can be deduced from the number of monthly active users on each platform. Pandora topped out at about 81 million monthly active users three years ago, and that number continues to decline as time passes. Pandora CFO Naveen Chopra even pointed out during the recent earnings conference call that “total monthly users have decreased about 4% year-over-year.”
As it relates to Apple Music, the company doesn’t publish a lot of information pertaining to monthly active user data. But you can see from the chart below that it is still continuing to gain momentum in this market segment. Spotify also continues to gain momentum, with its most recent report of monthly active users at 159 million – 36 million more than the year before.
Where’s the Profit?
Aside from the social movement taking shape, Pandora is also under financial pressure. Diving into Pandora’s recently filed 10-Q, you can see that YoY it has taken another loss and is still not profitable. This loss is essentially identical to what the company reported one year ago. Revenue in its most recently reported quarter came in at $319 million compared to $316 million last year. This comparison demonstrates almost 0% top-line growth. What’s more concerning is that the CFO mentions during the conference call that the company saw an uptick in “non-guaranteed” revenue. This category of revenue refers to sponsored listening and CPV video, which is complex and not easily forecast. This surprise uptick could have been what actually saved the overall revenue metric from a YoY decrease.
Moving down the income statement, you will also notice that content acquisition costs continue to rise. These costs are nearly 68% of revenue and, if not closely monitored, will inevitably lead to margin recession. Metrics like these are worrisome when considering what an income statement of a popular 18-year-old company should look like. In order for a company to pursue profitability, top-line growth should be substantially increasing followed by expanding margins so that the effects can be felt at the bottom-line level. When you tie together the user data graph above with stalled revenue growth and bad margins, you unfortunately get a story that ends with worse EPS numbers reported in the future.
Examining their balance sheet, you can foresee more problems ahead. While they do have cash, I don’t believe it will be sustainable in the long run. Flat and potentially near-term decreases in revenue due to immense industry competition and a steady decline in users will eventually result in smaller amounts of cash. As a matter of fact, this shrink in cash is already coming to fruition, as you can see below.
Cash on hand this quarter was $454 million, which is a decrease of about 9% from the same quarter one year ago. Pandora, while it does have enough liquidity to cover balance sheet debt currently, might be making it’s way toward trouble in this department further down the road. With its growth days behind it, it’s tough to imagine any tailwinds pushing Pandora to profitability.
Stock Enters Overreaction Territory
Pandora’s stock has recently seen a 21% gap up after the recent earnings announcement; I believe this is certainly an overreaction. One of the reasons justifying this overreaction is the syntax used during the conference call. The CEO was especially optimistic with his opening remarks and spoke about how exciting a time it is in the audio streaming space, making his best effort to reignite excitement in shareholders about the future. Another key piece of this quarter for investors is that Pandora beat EPS estimates. The company has been on a downward slide over the past year, with the stock price falling nearly 50%.
I believe the Street set expectations fairly low for this quarter. The earnings estimate published was a loss of $.33/share, so when Pandora beat with only a loss of $.27/share, long-time share holders were ecstatic. With an almost 20% bottom-line beat the stock traded on a volume of 46 million shares (nearly 3x the average daily volume). Given that nearly 30% of the float is short, this almost certainly caused many investors to cover their position. When there are that many shorts who are forced into covering their position, the result is a higher stock price.
Piecing Together the Puzzle
Putting these facts together, one can conclude that now is an ideal time to liquidate your position or go short. While the price appreciation might seem substantial, from a technical perspective I believe that this is just a classic gap fill dating back to November 2017. At that time, the gap in reference was created around $7 per share when Pandora reported a loss of $0.06. Pandora is currently trading right around $7 per share, hence filling the gap from November 2017. As we know, gaps don’t get filled 100% of the time. But for the most part, these gaps usually find a way of filling eventually.
In summary, I believe this new gap up of 21% based off the recent earnings report loss of $0.27/share (larger than in November) will ultimately end in the decline of Pandora’s stock price. When evaluating the company on a per-share basis vs. their competition and financial implications ahead, I believe an investment is better suited elsewhere.
Disclosure: I am/we are short P.
